Welcome

Welcome to the Serencog Free Full-Stack Development Bootcamp.

Over four lessons you will build one real project: your own personal portfolio website. You will write its structure with HTML, style it with CSS, make it interactive with JavaScript, save it with Git and publish it on the internet with GitHub Pages. At the end, you will get a first look at React, the tool many companies use to build modern web applications.

You do not need any programming experience. Every new word is explained the first time it appears, and every piece of code is explained line by line.

This handbook brings together everything from the bootcamp: the installation guide, the four lessons, the activities, the homework and the complete working code. Keep it. It is your reference during the bootcamp and long after it.

Your portfolio will be public. Anyone on the internet will be able to see it. Do not include your phone number, home address, ID number or date of birth. Use an email address you are happy to share. A photo is optional; an avatar is fine.

How to use this handbook

If you attend every lesson, use the handbook to revise after each class and to finish your homework.

If you miss a lesson, read that lesson’s part from the beginning and type the code yourself. Each lesson ends with the complete code at that point, so you can always catch up. The full, final code is in the Reference section.

If you get stuck, go to the “Common problems” table at the end of the lesson, or the Troubleshooting section in the Reference. Then ask in the WhatsApp Questions group, with a screenshot.

What the boxes mean

A new technical word, explained in plain English.

A shortcut or good habit that saves you time.

Something that often goes wrong, or that you must not skip.

A practical exercise. Do it on your own computer before reading on.

How code is shown

Code appears in dark boxes. The line above each box says which file the code goes in, and where:

index.html — inside <body>

<h1>I'm Amina Otieno</h1>

Type the code yourself rather than copying it, at least the first time. Your fingers learn faster than your eyes. Replace the sample name, Amina Otieno, and the sample text with your own.

Short pieces of code inside a sentence look like this: index.html.

Part 1Getting started: installation and setup

Before Lesson 1, you install five free tools and create one free account. Allow 60–90 minutes, and finish at least two days before Lesson 1, so there is time to get help if something goes wrong. Follow the steps in order.

Before you start

Check that you have these before installing anything:

  • A laptop or desktop computer running Windows 10 or 11, macOS (version 12 Monterey or newer is best) or Ubuntu Linux 22.04 or newer.
  • A stable internet connection. You will download about 1 GB in total.
  • At least 5 GB of free storage.
  • Permission to install software. On a work or school laptop, you may need to ask your IT department.
  • Your computer password. Installers may ask for it.
  • An email address you can open now. You need it to create a GitHub account.

Phones, tablets (including iPads) and Chromebooks are not suitable. If that is all you have, read the fallback plan at the end of this part and contact Serencog before Lesson 1.

The tools you will install, and why

Tool What it is Why you need it When you use it
Visual Studio Code (VS Code) A code editor: the program you write code in. Like Microsoft Word, but for code It colours your code and helps you spot mistakes Every lesson
Google Chrome A web browser You open your pages in it, and use its Developer Tools to inspect and fix them Every lesson
Node.js Lets your computer run JavaScript outside a browser Professional web tools, including React, depend on it. In the bootcamp you only test it Setup; the full programme
npm Installs automatically with Node.js. It downloads ready-made code packages Used in the full programme Setup; the full programme
Git Saves snapshots of your project, like save points in a video game You can go back if something breaks Lesson 4
GitHub account A website that stores your Git projects online It publishes your portfolio as a real website Lesson 4

You do not need to install React. Your instructor shows React at the end of the bootcamp.

Words you need to know

Terminal. A window where you control your computer by typing instead of clicking. You type a command, press Enter, and the computer replies with text.

How to open a terminal:

Computer The terminal is called How to open it
Windows PowerShell Press the Windows key, type PowerShell, press Enter
macOS Terminal Press Cmd+Space, type Terminal, press Enter
Ubuntu Terminal Press Ctrl+Alt+T
Any, inside VS Code VS Code terminal Menu Terminal → New Terminal, or press Ctrl+` (the backtick key, under Esc)

It is normal for the terminal to look plain and a little intimidating. You cannot break your computer by typing the commands in this handbook.

Command. A short instruction you type in the terminal, such as node -v (“show me the Node.js version”).

To run a command: click inside the terminal, type or paste the command (paste is Ctrl+V on Windows, Cmd+V on macOS, Ctrl+Shift+V in the Ubuntu terminal), then press Enter. When a box has several commands, run them one line at a time. Spaces and capital letters matter.

Code editor. A program for writing code. It saves plain text files, such as index.html, with no hidden formatting.

Word processors such as Word or TextEdit add hidden formatting that breaks code. Never write code in them.

File, folder and file extension. A file is one document, for example index.html. The part after the dot, .html, is the extension: it tells the computer what kind of file it is. A folder holds files. Your whole website lives in one folder.

Path. The address of a file, for example C:\Users\Amina\Documents\portfolio\index.html on Windows or /Users/amina/Documents/portfolio/index.html on macOS.

Windows: show file extensions. Windows hides them by default, which causes confusion. Open File Explorer → View → Show → File name extensions (Windows 11), or View → tick File name extensions (Windows 10).

PATH. When you type a command like node, your computer searches a list of folders for a program with that name. That list is the PATH. Installers add their folder to it for you.

If you see “node is not recognized” or “command not found” just after installing, the terminal is still using the old list. Close the terminal and open a new one. If that fails, restart the computer. Do not edit PATH by hand.

LTS (Long Term Support). The stable version of a program, recommended for most people. Always choose the LTS download for Node.js.

A version number such as v26.13.1 reads as major.minor.patch. For this bootcamp, the first number of your Node.js version should be 22 or higher.

Passwords are invisible in the terminal. On macOS and Ubuntu, when a command asks for your password, nothing appears as you type, not even dots. This is a security feature. Type your password and press Enter.

Install the tools

Do these in order. Only download from the official websites listed here. Each tool has steps for Windows, macOS and Ubuntu: follow only the ones for your computer.

Which Mac do I have? Apple menu → About This Mac. “Chip: Apple M…” means Apple Silicon; “Processor: Intel” means Intel. The downloads below work on both.

Tool 1: Visual Studio Code

What and why: the code editor you will use in every lesson. Official download: https://code.visualstudio.com/download

Windows

  1. Click Windows (the big button downloads the User Installer, which is the right one).
  2. Open the downloaded file from your Downloads folder.
  3. Accept the agreement and click Next until you reach Select Additional Tasks.
  4. Tick Add “Open with Code” action to Windows Explorer file context menu, the matching directory context menu option, and make sure Add to PATH is ticked (it usually is).
  5. Click Next → Install → Finish. VS Code opens.

macOS

  1. Click Mac (the Universal version works on all Macs).
  2. Open your Downloads folder in Finder. Double-click the .zip file if it has not opened by itself. You will see Visual Studio Code.
  3. Drag Visual Studio Code into the Applications folder. This matters: if you run it from Downloads, it will not update properly.
  4. Open it from Applications. If macOS warns that it was downloaded from the internet, click Open.
  5. Optional, useful later: in VS Code press Cmd+Shift+P, type shell command, and choose Shell Command: Install ‘code’ command in PATH.

Ubuntu

Run this in the terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T). It asks for your password:

sudo snap install code --classic

Then open Visual Studio Code from the app menu. If snap is not available, download the .deb file from the official page, then run cd ~/Downloads followed by sudo apt install ./code_*.deb.

Check it works: VS Code opens and shows a Welcome tab.

Tool 2: Google Chrome

What and why: the browser you open your pages in, with built-in Developer Tools. Official download: https://www.google.com/chrome/

If you already have Chrome, skip this tool.

  • Windows: click Download Chrome, open the downloaded file and let it install. Chrome opens when it finishes.
  • macOS: open the downloaded googlechrome.dmg, drag Google Chrome into Applications, then open it from there.
  • Ubuntu: run these three commands, one at a time:
cd ~/Downloads
wget https://dl.google.com/linux/direct/google-chrome-stable_current_amd64.deb
sudo apt install -y ./google-chrome-stable_current_amd64.deb

Chrome is only available for standard 64-bit Intel/AMD Linux computers. On ARM computers, such as a Raspberry Pi, use Chromium or Firefox instead.

Check it works: Chrome opens a web page.

Tool 3: Node.js (LTS) and npm

What and why: runs JavaScript outside the browser; npm installs code packages. npm comes with Node.js automatically. Official download: https://nodejs.org/en/download

Windows

  1. On the download page, make sure the version says LTS and choose the Windows Installer (.msi).
  2. Open the file. Click Next, accept the licence and keep the default folder.
  3. On the screen Tools for Native Modules, leave the box unticked. You do not need those tools, and they take a long time to install.
  4. Click Install, then Yes if Windows asks for permission, then Finish.

macOS

  1. On the download page, make sure the version says LTS and choose the macOS Installer (.pkg).
  2. Open the file and click Continue through the screens, then Install.
  3. Enter your Mac password when asked, then click Close.

Ubuntu

Do not use sudo apt install nodejs: it usually installs an old version. Use nvm (Node Version Manager), the method listed on the official Node.js download page. It needs no sudo. First install Git and curl (curl downloads files):

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git curl

Then install nvm:

curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.5/install.sh | bash

Close the terminal and open a new one (this step is essential), then install the LTS version of Node.js:

nvm install --lts

If the Node.js download page (Linux → nvm) shows a newer nvm version number than v0.40.5, you may use its command instead.

Check it works: see “Check the tools work” below.

Tool 4: Git

What and why: saves snapshots (commits) of your project. Used in Lesson 4.

Windows — official download: https://git-scm.com/downloads/win

  1. Click Click here to download (the 64-bit version) and open the file.
  2. The installer has many screens. Keep the default on every screen except these two:
    • Choosing the default editor used by Git: select Use Visual Studio Code as Git’s default editor. (The default, Vim, is hard for beginners to exit.)
    • Adjusting the name of the initial branch: select Override the default branch name and keep the word main.
  3. Click Install, then Finish.

macOS — Git comes with Apple’s free developer tools. Open Terminal and run:

xcode-select --install

A window appears. Click Install and accept the licence. The download can take 10–30 minutes. If the terminal says the command line tools are already installed, Git is already on your Mac. Alternative download: https://git-scm.com/downloads/mac

Ubuntu — you already installed Git with sudo apt install -y git curl in Tool 3.

Close every terminal window now. Quit PowerShell, Terminal and VS Code completely. New windows pick up the tools you just installed. If you have time, restart your computer: it prevents most “not recognized” problems.

Check the tools work

Open a new terminal and run each command. Your numbers may be different from the examples.

Command What it checks You should see
node -v Node.js is installed v26.13.1 or similar. The first number must be 22 or higher
npm -v npm is installed A version number, such as 11.6.2
npm ping npm can reach the internet A last line containing PONG
git --version Git is installed git version 2.51.0 or similar 
node -v
npm -v
npm ping
git --version

Windows: “npm.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system”. This is very common and easy to fix. Run the command below in PowerShell, type Y and press Enter if asked, then close PowerShell, open a new one and try npm -v again. It changes the setting only for your own user account.

Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned

If npm ping fails, your network may block npm (common on some office or campus networks). Try another network, such as a phone hotspot, and tell your instructor.

Take one screenshot of your terminal showing all four results, and send it to the WhatsApp Setup help group.

Set up Git and GitHub

These three steps make Lesson 4, when your portfolio goes live, much smoother.

Step 1: create a free GitHub account

GitHub. A website that stores Git projects online. It can also publish websites for free with GitHub Pages.

  1. Go to https://github.com/signup.
  2. Enter your email address, create a password and choose a username.
  3. Complete the puzzle check, then enter the code GitHub sends to your email.
  4. If GitHub offers a paid plan, choose Free. If it asks you to set up two-factor authentication, follow its steps; you will need your phone.

Choose your username carefully. It appears in your portfolio’s web address: https://username.github.io. Use something professional, such as your name (amina-otieno), not a nickname. Write down your username and keep your password safe.

Step 2: tell Git your name and email

Git labels every save point with your name and email. Use the same email as your GitHub account. Run these one at a time, replacing the example name and email with your own. Keep the quote marks.

git config --global user.name "Amina Otieno"
git config --global user.email "amina@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

These commands print nothing when they work. To check, run:

git config --global --list

You should see your details, including:

user.name=Amina Otieno
user.email=amina@example.com
init.defaultbranch=main

If the list ends with : or (END), press Q to get back to the prompt.

Step 3: stay signed in to GitHub in Chrome

Open https://github.com/login in Chrome and sign in. Leave it signed in. In Lesson 4, VS Code opens Chrome and asks you to Authorize it to publish your portfolio; being signed in already makes that one click.

Your first web page

This tests everything together, and it is exactly how you will work in class.

1. Create a project folder

Every website lives in its own folder. Create one in your Documents folder and name it serencog-hello (all lowercase, a dash instead of a space).

  • Windows: File Explorer (Windows+E) → Documents → right-click empty space → New → Folder.
  • macOS: Finder → Documents → File → New Folder (Cmd+Shift+N).
  • Ubuntu: Files → Documents → right-click empty space → New Folder.

No spaces or capital letters in web file names. Spaces cause problems in web addresses, and capital letters cause problems on web servers (you will see why in Lesson 4). Use lowercase and dashes: my-photo.jpg, not My Photo.JPG.

2. Open the folder in VS Code

  1. In VS Code, click File → Open Folder… (on macOS: File → Open…).
  2. Go to Documents, select serencog-hello and click Select Folder (Windows) or Open (macOS, Ubuntu).
  3. If VS Code asks “Do you trust the authors of the files in this folder?”, click Yes, I trust the authors. It is your own folder.

The left panel, the Explorer, now shows SERENCOG-HELLO. That is your project.

3. Create index.html

  1. In the Explorer, hover over SERENCOG-HELLO and click the New File icon (a page with a +).
  2. Type the name index.html exactly and press Enter. The file opens on the right.
  3. Type or paste this code:

index.html

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>My First Webpage</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello, Serencog!</h1>
  <p>I am ready to start learning web development.</p>
</body>
</html>
  1. Save: Ctrl+S (Windows, Ubuntu) or Cmd+S (macOS). A white dot on the file’s tab means “not saved yet”; it disappears when you save.

Don’t worry about what each line means yet. Lesson 1 explains all of it.

4. Open it in Chrome, then change it

  1. In VS Code’s Explorer, right-click index.html and choose Reveal in File Explorer (Windows), Reveal in Finder (macOS) or Open Containing Folder (Ubuntu).
  2. Right-click index.html in that window → Open with → Google Chrome. Or drag the file onto an open Chrome window.
  3. You should see a big heading, Hello, Serencog!, and the sentence below it.
  4. In VS Code, change Hello, Serencog! to Hello, I'm and your name. Save.
  5. Go back to Chrome and refresh: F5 (Windows, Ubuntu) or Cmd+R (macOS). Your name appears.

Edit → save → refresh. This is the loop you will use all bootcamp. If a change doesn’t appear, nine times out of ten you forgot to save.

5. Run JavaScript with Node.js

  1. In VS Code, create another new file called hello.js, type this line and save:

hello.js

console.log("Hello from Node.js! My setup works.");
  1. Open VS Code’s terminal: menu Terminal → New Terminal. A panel opens at the bottom, already inside your project folder.
  2. Run:
node hello.js

You should see Hello from Node.js! My setup works. If you see “Cannot find module”, the file was not saved or the terminal is in a different folder. Save the file, close the terminal (bin icon) and open a new one.

Understanding the project files and folders

Your bootcamp portfolio uses the same idea as serencog-hello, with a few more files. By Lesson 4 it looks like this:

portfolio/
├── index.html      the page: structure and content (Lesson 1)
├── style.css       how it looks (Lesson 2)
├── script.js       what it does (Lesson 3)
├── README.md       a description for GitHub (Lesson 4, optional)
└── images/
    └── profile.png your photo or avatar (optional)

index.html is a special name: when someone opens a website folder, browsers and web servers look for index.html first. It must be at the top level of the folder, not inside another folder.

Readiness checklist

Tick each item only after you have seen it work with your own eyes.

Prepare your portfolio content

Before Lesson 1, write these in a note on your phone or computer. Students who arrive with their own words spend Lesson 1 building, and the portfolio feels personal from the first minute.

  • A one-line description of yourself.
  • A 2–4 sentence “About me”.
  • 4–6 skills or interests. Non-tech skills count: teamwork, design, a language, football.
  • 1–2 things you have done: a school project, a business, an event, volunteering. Anything real.
  • Optional: a square photo or an avatar, saved as profile.png or profile.jpg.

If something goes wrong

On any computer

Problem What to do
“node / npm / git is not recognized” or “command not found” Close the terminal and open a new one. Still failing? Restart the computer. Still failing? Install that tool again. Do not edit PATH by hand; ask in the Setup help group
node -v shows v20 or lower Windows/macOS: download the LTS installer from nodejs.org and run it again. Ubuntu: run nvm install --lts, then nvm alias default 'lts/*', and open a new terminal
Chrome shows my code instead of a page, or the page is blank Check the file is called exactly index.html (on Windows, not index.html.txt). Save (no white dot), then refresh. Make sure you wrote the code in VS Code, not Word, TextEdit or Notepad
My change does not appear in Chrome Save in VS Code first, then refresh. Check Chrome’s address bar shows the file from the same folder you are editing
A strange editor opened in the terminal and I cannot get out This is usually Vim. Press Esc, type :q! and press Enter. If the screen shows (END) or :, press Q
npm ping fails or times out Try a different network (a phone hotspot works). On a work network, tell your instructor
“You need administrator permission” Ask the computer’s owner or IT department, or use another computer. See the fallback plan
My antivirus blocked an installer If you downloaded from the official links in this handbook, allow it and run it again. If unsure, ask first

Windows

Problem What to do
“npm.ps1 cannot be loaded…” Run Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned in PowerShell, type Y, open a new PowerShell. If your organisation blocks it, use Command Prompt (search for “cmd”) instead
“Windows protected your PC” Click More info → Run anyway, only for files from the official links
I chose the wrong options in the Git installer Run the installer again, or set the editor with git config --global core.editor "code --wait"

macOS

Problem What to do
“App can’t be opened because Apple cannot check it” System Settings → Privacy & Security → scroll down → Open Anyway. Only for apps from the official links
xcode-select --install says the software is “not currently available” Apple’s servers are busy. Wait an hour and try again, or install Git from git-scm.com/downloads/mac
VS Code says it is running from a read-only location It is still in Downloads. Quit it and drag it into Applications

Ubuntu

Problem What to do
nvm: command not found Close the terminal and open a new one. Still failing: run source ~/.bashrc
snap: command not found Use the .deb method in the VS Code step
“Unable to locate package” or apt errors Run sudo apt update first, then the install command again
“Permission denied” or EACCES errors from npm Do not use sudo npm. You do not need global npm installs for the bootcamp. Ask in the Setup help group

Still stuck? The fallback plan

Your own installed setup is the main way to take part. Use this only if it still does not work the day before Lesson 1, so you do not miss the start.

  1. Ask for help first. Post a screenshot of the error in the WhatsApp Setup help group, or join the online setup clinic before Lesson 1. Include your operating system, the step, the exact command and the error.
  2. Temporary option for Lessons 1–3: on any Windows, macOS or Linux computer with Chrome, open https://vscode.dev. It is VS Code running in the browser. Click Open Folder, pick your project folder and edit your files there. Nothing needs installing.
  3. For Lesson 4: you can publish your portfolio by uploading files on the GitHub website, without Git. Part 5 explains this “Plan B”.

The fallback is temporary. Keep working with the Serencog team until your installed setup works; you will need it in the full programme.

Part 2Lesson 1 — HTML: building the structure

Lesson 1 at a glance

What you build: the complete structure of your portfolio, with all seven parts (header and navigation, hero, About, Skills, Projects, Contact and footer) written in your own words. It is not styled yet; that comes in Lesson 2.

By the end of this lesson, you can:

  1. Explain in one sentence what HTML, CSS and JavaScript each do.
  2. Create a project folder, open it in VS Code and view an HTML file in Chrome.
  3. Write headings, paragraphs, links, images and lists.
  4. Use semantic elements (header, nav, main, section, article, footer) to structure a page.
  5. Build every section of your portfolio with your own content.

Activity: edit the internet

The lesson starts with a surprise: you change a real website.

Try it.

  1. Open any news website or a Wikipedia page in Chrome.
  2. Right-click the main headline and choose Inspect. A panel opens: Chrome’s Developer Tools (DevTools).
  3. In the Elements panel, the headline’s code is highlighted. Double-click the headline text, type a new headline with your name in it, and press Enter.
  4. The real website now shows your headline. Take a screenshot.
  5. Refresh the page. The original headline comes back.

You didn’t hack anything. Your browser downloaded a copy of the page, and you changed your copy. That copy is written in HTML, and today you write your own.

How websites work

When you type a web address, your browser is like a customer at a restaurant. It sends an order (a request) to a server, which is just a computer somewhere else: the kitchen. The kitchen sends back the food: files, usually HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Your browser reads those files and draws the page you see.

Browser. The program you use to open websites, such as Chrome. Chrome is the browser; Google is a website you visit with it.

Server. A computer that is always on and sends files to anyone who asks for them.

For now your files live on your own laptop and Chrome reads them directly. In Lesson 4 they go on a server.

HTML, CSS and JavaScript: a website is like a house

  • HTML is the structure: walls, rooms and doors. It says what is on the page: a heading, a paragraph, a picture.
  • CSS is the style: paint, furniture and decoration. It says how it looks.
  • JavaScript is the behaviour: the electricity. Lights switch on and doors open when you press a button.

HTML (HyperText Markup Language). The language that gives a web page its structure and content. It is not a programming language: it describes what each part of the page is.

Quick quiz. You want to make a button orange: HTML, CSS or JavaScript? You want a menu to open when someone taps it?

Answers: CSS; JavaScript.

Set up your portfolio project

  1. Create a folder called portfolio in Documents (lowercase).
  2. In VS Code: File → Open Folder → choose portfolio. The Explorer shows PORTFOLIO.
  3. Create a new file called index.html.
  4. In the empty file, type ! and press Enter. VS Code writes the whole starting code for you. This shortcut is called Emmet.
  5. Change the text inside <title> to your name, and save.

index.html — the starting point

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>Amina Otieno | Portfolio</title>
</head>
<body>

</body>
</html>

Line by line:

Code What it means
<!DOCTYPE html> Tells the browser “this is a modern HTML page”. Always the first line
<html lang="en"> … </html> Wraps the whole page. lang="en" says the page is in English, which helps screen readers and search engines
<head> … </head> Information about the page. Visitors don’t see most of it
<meta charset="UTF-8"> Lets the page show every letter and symbol correctly, including accents and emoji
<meta name="viewport" …> Makes the page fit phone screens properly. Never delete it: Lesson 2 depends on it
<title> … </title> The text on the browser tab
<body> … </body> Everything visitors see. It’s empty for now, so the page is blank

Open index.html in Chrome (right-click it in VS Code → Reveal in File Explorer / Reveal in Finder / Open Containing Folder, then open it with Chrome). The page is blank, but the tab shows your name. Change one word in the title, save, refresh, and watch the tab change. That’s the edit → save → refresh loop.

Tags, elements and attributes

HTML is made of elements. Most elements have three parts, like a sandwich: an opening tag, the content, and a closing tag with a slash.

Tag. A word in angle brackets that marks where an element starts or ends: <p> opens a paragraph, </p> closes it.

Element. The whole thing: opening tag, content and closing tag. <p>Hello</p> is a paragraph element.

Attribute. Extra information about an element, written inside the opening tag as name="value". In <a href="#projects">, the attribute href says where the link goes.

In the example above, a stands for “anchor”, HTML’s word for a link. Visitors see “See my work”; when they click it, they go to the Projects section.

Two rules to remember:

  • Attributes only ever go inside the opening tag.
  • Some elements have no content and no closing tag. They are called empty elements. <img> (an image) and <meta> are examples.

Headings and paragraphs

HTML has six heading levels, <h1> to <h6>. You will use three:

Element Use it for In your portfolio
<h1> The main heading. One per page Your name
<h2> A section title About Me, Skills, Projects, Contact
<h3> A title inside a section Each project’s title
<p> A paragraph of text Descriptions

Headings are an outline, not a font size. Don’t choose <h3> because it looks smaller. Size and colour come from CSS in Lesson 2.

Build the hero and About sections

The hero is the first thing visitors see: your photo, your name, one line about you and a button. Add this inside <body>:

index.html — inside <body>

<section id="hero">
  <img src="images/profile.png" alt="Portrait of Amina Otieno">
  <h1>I'm Amina Otieno</h1>
  <p>An aspiring web developer from Nairobi who loves turning ideas into websites.</p>
  <a href="#projects">See my work</a>
</section>

<section id="about">
  <h2>About Me</h2>
  <p>I studied business, and I am now learning web development with Serencog Technologies.</p>
</section>

Line by line:

  • <section id="hero"> starts a section of the page. The id gives it a unique name, so a link can jump to it later.
  • <img …> shows your picture (explained in the next section).
  • <h1> is your name: the page’s one main heading.
  • <p> is your one-line description.
  • <a href="#projects">See my work</a> is a link that jumps to the section with id="projects" (you build it later in this lesson).
  • </section> ends the section. The About section follows the same pattern, with an <h2>.

Replace the sample name and text with your own. Save and refresh.

Checkpoint. Your own name appears as a big heading in Chrome.

Images and alt text

The image line from the hero

<img src="images/profile.png" alt="Portrait of Amina Otieno">
  • img is an empty element: no content and no closing tag.
  • src (source) is the path to the picture, relative to index.html: inside the images folder, a file called profile.png.
  • alt (alternative text) describes the picture. Screen readers read it aloud to blind visitors, and it appears if the image fails to load.

To add your picture: in VS Code’s Explorer, create a folder called images inside portfolio, then drag your photo or avatar into it. Name it profile.png or profile.jpg, and make the src match.

The names must match exactly, including .png versus .jpg and capital letters. If your file is Profile.JPG, rename it to profile.jpg. This matters again in Lesson 4, when your site goes online.

No photo? That’s fine: the portfolio will be public, so an avatar is a good choice, or you can delete the line for now.

See alt text in action. Change the src to images/profil.png (a typo), save and refresh: the alt text appears instead of the picture. Change it back.

Lists: your Skills section

A list has two parts: <ul> wraps the whole list, and each <li> is one item. ul means unordered list: bullet points. If the order matters, like steps in a recipe, use <ol>, an ordered list, which numbers the items for you.

index.html — after the About section

<section id="skills">
  <h2>Skills</h2>
  <ul>
    <li>HTML</li>
    <li>CSS</li>
    <li>JavaScript</li>
    <li>Teamwork</li>
  </ul>
</section>
  • Every <li> must sit between <ul> and </ul>, and each needs its own closing </li>.
  • Lists inside sections are indented further, so it’s easy to see what is inside what.

Try it. Add 4–6 of your own skills or interests. Then change <ul> and </ul> to <ol> and </ol>, save and refresh to see numbers. Change it back.

Semantic HTML: labels on boxes

Semantic HTML. Elements whose names describe the meaning of a part of the page, such as <header>, <nav> and <footer>.

These tags don’t change how the page looks. They tell browsers, search engines and screen readers what each part is, like labels on boxes when you move house: “kitchen”, “bedroom”, “books”. A screen reader can jump straight to the navigation, and Google understands which part is the main content.

Element Meaning In your portfolio
<header> The top bar of the page Your name (logo) and the menu
<nav> Navigation: the main menu links Links to About, Skills, Projects, Contact
<main> The main content, once per page Everything between the header and footer
<section> A themed part of the page, usually with a heading Hero, About, Skills, Projects, Contact
<article> A self-contained item that makes sense on its own Each project card
<footer> The bottom bar Copyright line

Game: name that box. Look at the screenshot at the start of this lesson. For each area (the top bar, the menu, a project card, the bottom bar), say which element it should be.

Header and navigation

Add the header above your hero section, then wrap all your sections in <main>:

index.html — the top of <body>

<header>
  <a href="#hero">Amina.</a>
  <nav>
    <ul>
      <li><a href="#about">About</a></li>
      <li><a href="#skills">Skills</a></li>
      <li><a href="#projects">Projects</a></li>
      <li><a href="#contact">Contact</a></li>
    </ul>
  </nav>
</header>

<main>
  <!-- hero, about and skills sections go here -->
  • The first link, Amina., is your “logo”. It jumps back to the top (the hero).
  • The menu is a list of links inside <nav>. Each href starts with # and matches a section’s id.
  • <!-- … --> is a comment: a note for humans. Browsers ignore it.

Three kinds of links

<a href="#projects">See my work</a>
<a href="mailto:amina@example.com">amina@example.com</a>
<a href="https://github.com">GitHub</a>
Starts with Kind of link What it does
# In-page link Jumps to the element with that id on the same page
mailto: Email link Opens the visitor’s email app with your address filled in
https:// External link Goes to another website

External links need https://. Without it, www.github.com makes the browser look for a file with that name in your folder.

Projects

Each project is an <article>: a self-contained card. Add this after the Skills section:

index.html — after the Skills section

<section id="projects">
  <h2>Projects</h2>
  <article>
    <h3>My Portfolio</h3>
    <p>The website you are looking at, built during the Serencog Free Bootcamp.</p>
  </article>
  <article>
    <h3>Coming soon: my full-stack app</h3>
    <p>My next project: a complete web application with a backend and database.</p>
  </article>
</section>

The “Coming soon” card is on purpose: it shows visitors where you’re heading. Add a card for anything real you’ve done, even a non-tech project.

Contact: an email link and a form

index.html — after the Projects section

<section id="contact">
  <h2>Contact</h2>
  <p>Email me at <a href="mailto:amina@example.com">amina@example.com</a></p>
  <form id="contact-form" novalidate>
    <label for="name">Name</label>
    <input type="text" id="name">
    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input type="email" id="email">
    <label for="message">Message</label>
    <textarea id="message" rows="4"></textarea>
    <button type="submit">Send</button>
    <p id="form-message"></p>
  </form>
</section>
Code What it does
<a href="mailto:…"> Opens an email app. Use an address you’re happy to make public
<form id="contact-form" novalidate> Groups the form fields. The id and novalidate are used in Lesson 3: leave them as they are
<label for="name"> The visible name of a field. Its for matches the input’s id, so clicking the label selects the box, and screen readers read the label
<input type="text"> A one-line text box. type="email" is a box for an email address
<textarea rows="4"> A bigger box for a message, 4 lines tall
<button type="submit"> The Send button
<p id="form-message"></p> Empty on purpose. In Lesson 3, JavaScript writes messages into it

This form does not send messages. It is only the structure. In Lesson 3 you’ll check what visitors type, but sending a message needs a server, which is part of the full programme. Your email link is how visitors really contact you.

Footer

After </main>, add the footer:

<footer>
  <p>&copy; 2026 Amina Otieno. Built during the Serencog Free Bootcamp.</p>
</footer>

&copy; is an HTML entity: a code for a special character. It shows the © symbol.

How the sections fit together

Every element sits inside another, like boxes inside boxes. This outline shows the shape of your whole page:

<html>
├── <head>      title, character set, viewport
└── <body>
    ├── <header>    logo link + <nav> menu
    ├── <main>
    │   ├── <section id="hero">      photo, h1, line, button
    │   ├── <section id="about">     h2, paragraph
    │   ├── <section id="skills">    h2, list
    │   ├── <section id="projects">  h2, two <article> cards
    │   └── <section id="contact">   h2, email link, form
    └── <footer>    copyright line

The menu links in the header jump to the ids of the sections in main. Click Projects in your menu: the page jumps there. Your page now behaves like a real website.

index.html — complete at the end of Lesson 1

Bug hunt: find the 4 bugs

Find the four mistakes in this code before you read the answers.

<section id="about">
  <h2>About Me</h2
  <p>I love design and solving problems.
  <img src="images/profile.png">
  <a href=#contact>Contact me</a>
</section>

Answers:

  1. </h2 is missing its closing >.
  2. The <p> is never closed with </p>.
  3. The <img> has no alt text. Screen readers and slow connections need it.
  4. The href value has no quote marks. Use href="#contact".

The fixed version

<section id="about">
  <h2>About Me</h2>
  <p>I love design and solving problems.</p>
  <img src="images/profile.png" alt="Portrait of Amina Otieno">
  <a href="#contact">Contact me</a>
</section>

Let VS Code help. Unclosed tags change colour. Right-click → Format Document tidies the indentation, which makes missing closing tags easy to spot.

Common problems in Lesson 1

Problem How to fix it
Nothing changes in Chrome Save first (look for the white dot on the tab), then refresh. Tip: File → Auto Save
Tags look broken; text in the wrong place A closing tag or > is missing. Use Format Document
The image doesn’t show The folder and file names must match exactly: .png vs .jpg, capital letters
Headings look odd One h1, then h2 for sections. Size comes from CSS
Spaces or capitals in file names Rename to lowercase with dashes: profile.jpg
Chrome shows an old version Check Chrome’s address bar shows the same folder you’re editing in VS Code
Clicking a label doesn’t select its box Make for and id identical: for="email" and id="email"

Check your understanding

  1. Which language gives a page its structure?
  2. Which element should wrap your project cards: article or footer?
  3. What is alt text for?

Answers: (1) HTML. (2) article. (3) It describes an image for screen readers, and appears if the image doesn’t load.

  1. Finish any section you did not complete. Replace all the sample text with your own words.
  2. Add a third project card if you have something to show, even a non-tech project.
  3. Post a screenshot of your full page in the WhatsApp Show your work group. That earns your Builder badge.

Glossary

Short, simple definitions of the technical words in this handbook, in alphabetical order.

Term Meaning
addEventListener A JavaScript method that waits for an event, such as a click, on an element and runs a function when it happens
Alt text The alt attribute of an image: a short description read by screen readers and shown if the image fails to load
API Application Programming Interface: the agreed way for different parts of an application, such as a frontend and a backend, to talk to each other
Attribute Extra information inside an opening tag, written as name="value", such as href="#about"
Backend The part of an application that runs on a server and processes requests, out of sight
Boolean A value that is either true or false
Box model The idea that every element is a box made of content, padding, border and margin
Branch A line of work in a Git repository. The main one is usually called main
Browser The program you use to open websites, such as Chrome
Class A label added to HTML elements with class="…", so CSS and JavaScript can find them. Many elements can share a class
Commit A save point in Git: a snapshot of your project, with a message
Component In React, a reusable, named piece of a user interface, written as a function
Console A panel in Chrome’s DevTools where you can run JavaScript and read errors
const Creates a variable whose value stays the same
CSS Cascading Style Sheets: the language that controls how a page looks
Database An organised store of information that an application reads and writes
Declaration One CSS property and its value, such as color: #17356f;
defer An attribute on the <script> tag that makes JavaScript wait until the HTML has loaded
Deployment Putting a website on a server so it is live
DevTools Chrome’s Developer Tools, opened with F12 or right-click → Inspect
Domain name The easy-to-read name of a server, such as github.io
DOM Document Object Model: the browser’s live tree of a page’s elements, which JavaScript can change
Element A part of an HTML page: an opening tag, content and a closing tag
Emmet A VS Code shortcut. Typing ! and Enter writes the HTML starting code
Event Something that happens on the page, such as a click or a form being submitted
Flexbox A CSS layout tool that lines up the boxes inside a container in a row or column
Frontend The part of an application that people see and use in their browser
Full-stack Working on both the frontend and the backend of an application
Function A named set of instructions you write once and run whenever you call it
Git A version control tool on your computer that saves commits
GitHub A website that stores Git repositories online and can publish websites
GitHub Pages GitHub’s free hosting for websites stored in a repository
Grid A CSS layout tool that arranges boxes in rows and columns
HEX code A code for one exact colour, such as #17356f
Hosting Having your website stored on a web server
:hover A CSS state that applies styles while the mouse is over an element
HTML HyperText Markup Language: the language that gives a page its structure
ID A unique name for one element, added with id="…". In-page links and CSS can target it with #
JavaScript The programming language that makes web pages respond to visitors
JSX HTML-like code written inside JavaScript, used in React
let Creates a variable whose value can change
Library Ready-made code you add to your project
Live website A website anyone can open at its URL
localStorage Small storage in the visitor’s browser that remembers data after a refresh
Margin Space outside an element’s border, between boxes
Media query CSS rules that apply only when the screen matches a condition, such as being narrow
Node.js A program that runs JavaScript outside the browser
npm A tool, installed with Node.js, that downloads code packages
Operator A symbol that works with values, such as +, === or !
Padding Space inside an element’s border, around its content
Parameter An input a function receives, written in its brackets
Path The address of a file, such as images/profile.png
Props In React, the information passed into a component
Pull Bring changes down from a remote repository
Push Send your commits up to a remote repository
React A JavaScript library for building user interfaces from components
README A file, usually README.md, that explains a project on its repository page
Repository (repo) A project folder tracked by Git, with its history. Local on your computer, remote on GitHub
Responsive design Designing pages that work well on every screen size
Selector The part of a CSS rule that chooses which elements to style
Semantic HTML Elements whose names describe meaning, such as header, nav and footer
Server A computer that is always on and sends files to anyone who asks
Staging Choosing which changes go into the next commit (git add)
State In React, information that can change while the page is open
String A piece of text in quote marks, such as "Amina"
Tag A word in angle brackets that marks where an element starts or ends, such as <p> and </p>
Terminal A window where you type commands to your computer
Transition A CSS property that makes a change happen smoothly over time
URL The full address of a web page, such as https://amina.github.io/portfolio/
User interface (UI) The parts of an app that people see and interact with
Validation Checking what someone typed before using it
Variable A named box that holds a value
Version control A system that keeps an organised history of a project’s changes
Viewport The visible area of a web page on a screen. The viewport <meta> tag makes pages fit phones
VS Code Visual Studio Code: the code editor used in the bootcamp

Reference

A. Project folder structure

Your portfolio is one folder, with the HTML, CSS and JavaScript files side by side at the top level. The bootcamp did not use separate css/ and js/ folders: if you add them later, change the paths in <link href="…"> and <script src="…"> to match.

portfolio/
├── index.html      structure and content
├── style.css       styling, linked in <head>
├── script.js       interactivity, linked in <head> with defer
├── README.md       optional: describes the project on GitHub
└── images/
    └── profile.png your photo or avatar (optional)
